emergency.ateAvocado.steps[0].title: Step 1: Determine What Was Ingested
emergency.ateAvocado.steps[0].content: Check if the pit was swallowed. The flesh alone causes mild GI upset, but the pit is a life-threatening obstruction hazard.
emergency.ateAvocado.steps[1].title: Step 2: Do NOT Induce Vomiting If Pit Was Swallowed
emergency.ateAvocado.steps[1].content: ⚠️ If your dog ate the pit, do NOT induce vomiting — it can lodge in the esophagus on the way back up, causing worse obstruction.
emergency.ateAvocado.steps[2].title: Step 3: Watch for Guacamole Ingredients
emergency.ateAvocado.steps[2].content: If your dog ate guacamole, check the ingredients — onion, garlic, lime, and salt are additional toxins. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435.
emergency.ateAvocado.steps[3].title: Step 4: Monitor for Symptoms
emergency.ateAvocado.steps[3].content: Watch for vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, difficulty defecating (sign of obstruction), and lethargy. Symptoms usually appear within 2-12 hours.
emergency.ateAvocado.science.content: Avocado (Persea americana) contains persin, a fungicidal fatty acid derivative. Dogs are relatively resistant to persin compared to birds, rabbits, and horses, which can suffer fatal heart damage. In dogs, persin causes mild gastrointestinal irritation — vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. The greater clinical concern is the pit, which measures 3-5 cm and can cause intestinal obstruction, particularly in dogs under 20kg. The high fat content of the flesh (15-20%) also increases pancreatitis risk in predisposed breeds (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateAvocado.toxicityData.minimu: Flesh low toxicity — mild GI upset at any amount
emergency.ateAvocado.toxicityData.ld50: LD50: Persin exact LD50 unknown in dogs; pit obstruction is the primary clinical concern, not systemic toxicity
emergency.ateAvocado.toxicityData.source: Source: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center; Buoro et al., 1994
emergency.ateAvocado.toxicityData.exampl: Example: A 10kg dog eating avocado flesh will usually have mild GI signs; a swallowed pit of 3-5 cm can obstruct the small intestine.
emergency.ateAvocado.timeline[0].descrip: Mild GI signs from flesh: vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain
emergency.ateAvocado.timeline[1].descrip: Obstruction signs from pit: vomiting, straining to defecate, abdominal pain, lethargy
emergency.ateAvocado.timeline[2].descrip: Risk window: untreated obstruction can progress to intestinal perforation or necrosis
emergency.ateAvocado.faqs[0].question: Are avocados toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateAvocado.faqs[0].answer: Avocado contains persin, a fungicidal toxin that is mildly toxic to dogs. The flesh causes mild GI upset in most dogs, but the pit (seed) poses a far greater danger as it can cause life-threatening intestinal obstruction. The skin and leaves also contain higher persin concentrations than the flesh.
emergency.ateAvocado.faqs[1].question: What should I do if my dog ate an avocado pit?
emergency.ateAvocado.faqs[1].answer: If your dog swallowed an avocado pit, contact your vet immediately. The pit is large enough to cause intestinal blockage, especially in small and medium dogs. Do NOT induce vomiting — the pit can lodge in the esophagus on the way back up. Your vet will X-ray to locate the pit and determine if surgical removal is needed.
emergency.ateAvocado.faqs[2].question: How much avocado is dangerous for dogs?
emergency.ateAvocado.faqs[2].answer: The flesh has low toxicity — most dogs experience only mild vomiting or diarrhea from eating avocado flesh. However, the pit is a choking hazard and obstruction risk regardless of amount. The leaves and skin contain higher persin levels and should be avoided. Pancreatitis risk increases with large amounts due to high fat content.
emergency.ateAvocado.faqs[3].question: Can dogs eat guacamole?
emergency.ateAvocado.faqs[3].answer: No, guacamole is especially dangerous for dogs because it typically contains onion, garlic, lime juice, and salt — all of which are toxic to dogs. Onion and garlic cause hemolytic anemia, salt can cause ion poisoning, and lime peel contains essential oils. Call your vet immediately if your dog ate guacamole.

📞 Call vet or poison control immediately
emergency.ateCaffeine.steps[0].title: Step 1: Act Fast — Caffeine Absorbs Quickly
emergency.ateCaffeine.steps[0].content: Remove any remaining caffeine source. Caffeine is absorbed within 30-60 minutes — time is critical for decontamination.
emergency.ateCaffeine.steps[1].title: Step 2: Call Poison Control or Vet Immediately
emergency.ateCaffeine.steps[1].content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Have the product label ready to report caffeine content in mg.
emergency.ateCaffeine.steps[2].title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting If Symptoms Present
emergency.ateCaffeine.steps[2].content: ⚠️ If your dog shows trembling, hyperactivity, or seizures, inducing vomiting risks aspiration. Only induce if instructed by a professional AND your dog is asymptomatic within 30 minutes of ingestion.
emergency.ateCaffeine.steps[3].title: Step 4: Monitor Heart and Breathing
emergency.ateCaffeine.steps[3].content: Watch for rapid breathing, restlessness, and elevated heart rate. Caffeine causes cardiac arrhythmias — if your dog collapses or has difficulty breathing, go to emergency vet NOW.
emergency.ateCaffeine.science.content: Caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) is an adenosine receptor antagonist and phosphodiesterase inhibitor. In dogs, it causes central nervous system stimulation, cardiac muscle contraction, and smooth muscle relaxation. Dogs metabolize caffeine much slower than humans — half-life in dogs is 4.5 hours vs 3 hours in humans. This prolongs toxic effects. At high doses, caffeine causes excessive catecholamine release leading to tachycardia, fibrillation, and potentially death (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateCaffeine.toxicityData.sourc: Source: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center
emergency.ateCaffeine.toxicityData.examp: Example: 1-2 caffeine pills (200mg each) can cause serious symptoms in a small dog under 10kg.
emergency.ateCaffeine.timeline[0].descri: Early signs: restlessness, hyperactivity, vomiting, elevated heart rate
emergency.ateCaffeine.timeline[1].descri: Severe signs: tremors, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, collapse
emergency.ateCaffeine.timeline[2].descri: Resolution with treatment: hospitalization typically required 24-48 hours; good prognosis with early care
emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs[0].question: How much caffeine is toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs[0].answer: Mild symptoms appear at 20mg/kg of body weight. Severe toxicity occurs at 60mg/kg. The lethal dose (LD50) is approximately 140mg/kg. For a 20kg dog, this equals roughly 2,800mg of caffeine — about 28 cups of coffee. However, even small amounts (1-2 caffeine pills of 200mg each) can cause serious symptoms in small dogs.
emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms of caffeine poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 1-2 hours and include: restlessness, hyperactivity, vomiting, elevated heart rate, tremors, seizures, and collapse. Caffeine is absorbed rapidly and affects the central nervous system and cardiovascular system. Severe cases cause cardiac arrhythmias that can be fatal.
emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs[2].question: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate caffeine?
emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs[2].answer: Inducing vomiting may be recommended if ingestion occurred within 30 minutes and your dog is alert. However, caffeine is rapidly absorbed and can cause seizures — never induce vomiting if your dog shows any neurological symptoms. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 for guidance.
emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs[3].question: What is the treatment for caffeine poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs[3].answer: Treatment includes: induced vomiting (if early), activated charcoal to reduce absorption, IV fluids for elimination, anti-arrhythmic medications for heart issues, anti-seizure medications, and temperature regulation. Hospitalization is typically required for 24-48 hours. Prognosis is good with early treatment.

emergency.ateAlcohol.meta.keywords: my dog drank alcohol, alcohol toxicity dogs, dog drank beer, dog ate wine, dog ethanol poisoning, alcohol dangerous for dogs
emergency.ateAlcohol.banner.title: My Dog Drank Alcohol: Emergency Guide
emergency.ateAlcohol.banner.subtitle: Alcohol (ethanol) is a potent CNS depressant in dogs. Even small amounts cause ataxia, depression, and metabolic acidosis. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately.
emergency.ateAlcohol.article.headline: My Dog Drank Alcohol: Emergency Guide

emergency.ateAlcohol.article.ogTitle: My Dog Drank Alcohol: Emergency Guide | petsMetrics
emergency.ateAlcohol.article.ogDescripti: What to do if your dog drinks alcohol.
emergency.ateAlcohol.steps[0].title: Step 1: Remove All Alcohol Immediately
emergency.ateAlcohol.steps[0].content: Take away any remaining beverages, food containing alcohol, or raw bread dough. Clean up any spills — dogs may lick floors.
emergency.ateAlcohol.steps[1].title: Step 2: Assess Your Dog's Neurological State
emergency.ateAlcohol.steps[1].content: Check: Can your dog walk normally? Are they alert or depressed? Vomiting? If your dog cannot stand or is unconscious — go to emergency vet NOW.
emergency.ateAlcohol.steps[2].title: Step 3: Call Poison Control
emergency.ateAlcohol.steps[2].content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Calculate approximate alcohol consumed in grams: volume (mL) × alcohol% × 0.789 = grams of ethanol.
emergency.ateAlcohol.steps[3].title: Step 4: Keep Your Dog Safe
emergency.ateAlcohol.steps[3].content: Prevent falls due to ataxia. Keep your dog warm — alcohol causes vasodilation and hypothermia. Do NOT leave them unattended. Monitor breathing and consciousness every 15 minutes.
emergency.ateAlcohol.science.content: Ethanol (C2H5OH) is absorbed rapidly from the GI tract and crosses the blood-brain barrier within minutes. Dogs lack efficient alcohol dehydrogenase enzymes, making them 3-5 times more sensitive than humans. Ethanol inhibits NMDA receptors and enhances GABA activity, causing CNS depression, respiratory depression, and metabolic acidosis. The lethal dose in dogs is 5.5 mL/kg of pure ethanol. Raw bread dough is doubly dangerous — yeast fermentation continues in the warm stomach, producing more alcohol and expanding the dough (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateAlcohol.toxicityData.minimu: As little as 1.5 mL/kg of pure ethanol can cause noticeable intoxication
emergency.ateAlcohol.toxicityData.source: Source: Merck Veterinary Manual; ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center
emergency.ateAlcohol.toxicityData.exampl: Example: A single 12oz beer (5% ABV = 17g ethanol) can cause severe intoxication in a small dog under 10kg.
emergency.ateAlcohol.timeline[0].descrip: Early signs: disorientation, ataxia (wobbly gait), vomiting, depression
emergency.ateAlcohol.timeline[1].descrip: Severe signs: slowed breathing, metabolic acidosis, hypothermia, hypoglycemia (especially small dogs/puppies)
emergency.ateAlcohol.timeline[2].descrip: Resolution with supportive care: IV fluids, glucose, blood pH monitoring; unmonitored cases risk coma or death
emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs[0].question: Is alcohol toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs[0].answer: Yes, alcohol (ethanol) is highly toxic to dogs. The lethal dose is 5.5 mL/kg of pure ethanol. Dogs are much more sensitive than humans because they lack efficient alcohol dehydrogenase enzymes. Even small amounts cause ataxia, depression, and metabolic acidosis. Beer, wine, liquor, and raw bread dough all pose serious risks.
emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms of alcohol poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 30-90 minutes: disorientation, loss of coordination (ataxia), vomiting, depression, slowed breathing, metabolic acidosis, and in severe cases, coma and death. Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is a dangerous complication, especially in small dogs and puppies.
emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs[2].question: Can beer kill a dog?
emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs[2].answer: Yes, beer can kill a dog. A single 12oz beer (5% alcohol = 17g ethanol) can cause severe intoxication in a small dog (under 10kg). Dogs metabolize alcohol much slower than humans, so effects accumulate. Carbonation also speeds absorption. Never intentionally give alcohol to dogs.
emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs[3].question: What should I do if my dog accidentally drank alcohol?
emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs[3].answer: Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 or your vet immediately. Do NOT induce vomiting if your dog shows neurological symptoms (depression, ataxia). Remove any remaining alcohol. Keep your dog warm and safe from falls. Your vet may need to administer IV fluids, glucose, and monitor blood pH.

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.banner.subtit: Macadamia nuts are uniquely toxic to dogs — the toxin is unknown but causes hind leg weakness, tremors, and high fever. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 for immediate guidance.

👀 Monitor for symptoms, call vet if concerned
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.steps[0].titl: Step 1: Don't Panic, But Act Quickly
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.steps[0].cont: Remove any remaining macadamia nuts from your dog's reach. Stay calm — your dog will pick up on your stress.
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.steps[1].titl: Step 2: Do NOT Induce Vomiting (Unless Instructed)
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.steps[1].cont: ⚠️ Inducing vomiting can cause aspiration pneumonia. Only induce vomiting if explicitly instructed by a veterinarian or poison control.

Note the time of ingestion (check security camera footage if available)

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.science.conte: Macadamia nuts contain an unidentified toxin that uniquely affects dogs' neuromuscular system. The compound causes reversible weakness and ataxia in hind limbs, likely through disruption of motor neuron signaling. Unlike many toxins, the exact mechanism remains unknown despite decades of clinical observation. Research by Morton (2002) established the LD50 at 2.4 g/kg. The toxin is heat-stable and present in all forms: raw, roasted, salted, and in baked goods. Symptoms are dose-dependent and typically resolve within 12-48 hours with supportive care (ASPCA, 2023).
Minimum toxic dose: 0.5 g/kg body weight (mild symptoms)
Source: Morton, 2002 — Journal of Veterinary Diagnostic Investigation
Example: A 15kg (33lb) dog eating 15g of macadamia nuts (approximately 12-15 nuts) would reach the minimum toxic threshold. A typical nut weighs about 1.2-1.5g.
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.timeline[0].d: Early signs: weakness in hind legs, ataxia (wobbly gait), vomiting
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.timeline[1].d: Progression: tremors, reluctance to stand, abdominal pain, elevated temperature (up to 104°F/40°C)
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.timeline[2].d: Resolution: symptoms typically resolve with supportive care; full recovery expected
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[0].quest: Are macadamia nuts toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[0].answe: Yes, macadamia nuts are uniquely toxic to dogs. The exact toxin is unknown, but even small amounts cause weakness in hind legs, vomiting, tremors, and hyperthermia. The minimum toxic dose is approximately 2.4 g/kg of body weight. Most dogs recover within 48 hours with supportive veterinary care.
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[1].quest: How many macadamia nuts are dangerous for a dog?
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[1].answe: For a 20kg (44lb) dog, as few as 10-12 nuts can cause symptoms. Smaller dogs may react to just 2-3 nuts. The toxic threshold is approximately 0.5g of nuts per kg of body weight for mild symptoms, with severe symptoms appearing at 2.4g/kg.
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[2].quest: How long after eating macadamia nuts will my dog show symptoms?
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[2].answe: Symptoms typically appear within 3-12 hours after ingestion. The earliest sign is usually weakness or paralysis of the hind legs, followed by vomiting, tremors, abdominal pain, and elevated body temperature (up to 104°F/40°C).
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[3].quest: Can a dog die from eating macadamia nuts?
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[3].answe: Fatalities from macadamia nut poisoning are extremely rare. The LD50 is 2.4g/kg, meaning a 20kg dog would need to eat approximately 48g of nuts (about 40-50 nuts) to reach dangerous levels. However, even sub-lethal doses cause significant discomfort and require veterinary monitoring.
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[4].quest: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate macadamia nuts?
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[4].answe: Do NOT induce vomiting unless instructed by a veterinarian. Induction is only effective within 30 minutes of ingestion and can cause aspiration pneumonia. Contact ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 for specific guidance based on the amount consumed and time elapsed.

emergency.ateMushrooms.article.headline: My Dog Ate a Mushroom in the Yard: Emergency Guide
emergency.ateMushrooms.article.descripti: Emergency guide for wild mushroom toxicity in dogs: Amanita poisoning, liver failure risk, and immediate treatment.

emergency.ateMushrooms.article.ogDescrip: Emergency guide: Wild mushrooms can cause fatal liver failure in dogs. Act immediately.
emergency.ateMushrooms.banner.title: My Dog Ate a Mushroom in the Yard: What to Do Now
emergency.ateMushrooms.banner.subtitle: Wild mushrooms can cause fatal liver failure — symptoms are DELAYED 6-24 hours. Do not wait for symptoms. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 IMMEDIATELY.
emergency.ateMushrooms.riskAssessment.ro: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — do not wait
emergency.ateMushrooms.steps[0].title: THIS IS A TRUE EMERGENCY
emergency.ateMushrooms.steps[0].content: Do NOT wait for symptoms. Amatoxin poisoning has a deceptive delay — your dog looks fine for 6-24 hours while the toxin destroys the liver. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 NOW.
emergency.ateMushrooms.steps[1].title: Collect a Mushroom Sample
emergency.ateMushrooms.steps[1].content: If safe, collect remaining mushroom pieces (including base/bulb). Place in a paper bag (not plastic). This helps mycologists identify the species and determine toxicity risk.
emergency.ateMushrooms.steps[2].title: Go to Emergency Vet for Decontamination
emergency.ateMushrooms.steps[2].content: Your vet will induce vomiting (if within 2 hours), administer activated charcoal, and start IV fluids. They will monitor liver enzymes for 48-72 hours. Early treatment is the ONLY effective defense.
emergency.ateMushrooms.steps[3].title: Prepare for Hospitalization
emergency.ateMushrooms.steps[3].content: If amatoxin poisoning is confirmed, treatment includes: Penicillin G, Silymarin (milk thistle), N-acetylcysteine, IV fluids, and potentially plasma transfusions. Hospitalization typically lasts 3-7 days.
emergency.ateMushrooms.science.content: Amatoxins (alpha-amanitin, beta-amanitin) are bicyclic octapeptides found in Amanita, Galerina, and Lepiota species. They inhibit RNA polymerase II, halting protein synthesis in hepatocytes. The liver is the primary target because amatoxins undergo enterohepatic recirculation. After ingestion, there is a 6-12 hour latent period, followed by a gastroenteritis phase, a brief false recovery (12-24 hours), then fulminant liver failure with coagulopathy, encephalopathy, and death. Treatment within 12 hours has a 90% survival rate; after 24 hours, survival drops to 30% (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateMushrooms.toxicityData.exam: A single Amanita phalloides cap contains enough amatoxin to kill a 10-20kg dog. Partial ingestion is still life-threatening.
emergency.ateMushrooms.timeline[0].descr: Latent phase: dog appears normal. Toxin is being absorbed.
emergency.ateMushrooms.timeline[1].descr: Gastroenteritis phase: explosive vomiting and diarrhea begin. This is the BEST treatment window.
emergency.ateMushrooms.timeline[2].descr: False recovery: symptoms temporarily improve. Owners think dog is healing — FALSE sense of security.
emergency.ateMushrooms.timeline[3].descr: Fulminant liver failure: jaundice, bleeding disorders, hepatic encephalopathy, death without aggressive treatment.
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs[0].question: Are wild mushrooms toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs[0].answer: Many wild mushroom species are extremely toxic to dogs. The most dangerous is Amanita phalloides (Death Cap), which contains amatoxins that cause irreversible liver failure. Other toxic genera include Galerina, Lepiota, and Cortinarius. Even non-lethal species can cause severe GI upset. ANY mushroom ingestion should be treated as an emergency because you cannot reliably identify species in the field.
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs[1].question: How long after eating a mushroom will my dog show symptoms?
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms from amatoxin-containing mushrooms (Amanita) are DELAYED 6-24 hours. A dog appears fine initially, then develops explosive vomiting and diarrhea. After a brief "false recovery" of 12-24 hours, liver failure begins. By the time jaundice appears, damage is often irreversible. Other species cause symptoms within 30 minutes to 6 hours.
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs[2].question: What should I do if my dog ate a wild mushroom?
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs[2].answer: Treat EVERY wild mushroom ingestion as a life-threatening emergency. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately. Your vet will induce vomiting (if within 2 hours), administer activated charcoal, and admit for 48-72 hour observation with liver enzyme monitoring. Do NOT wait for symptoms — early treatment is the only effective defense against amatoxin poisoning.
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs[3].question: Can a dog die from eating a mushroom?
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs[3].answer: Yes. Amanita phalloides (Death Cap) has a 50-100% mortality rate in dogs without treatment. Amatoxins destroy liver cells by inhibiting RNA polymerase II. Even with treatment, mortality remains 20-30%. The lethal dose is 0.1mg/kg of amatoxin — a single Death Cap cap contains 10-15mg. Early aggressive treatment (within 12 hours) significantly improves survival.
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs[4].question: Can dogs eat store-bought mushrooms?
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs[4].answer: Store-bought mushrooms (white button, cremini, portobello) are generally safe for dogs in small amounts. However, they offer little nutritional value and can cause GI upset if fed in large quantities or cooked with butter/oil/garlic. Never assume a field mushroom is safe — only eat mushrooms you purchased from a grocery store.

emergency.ateMushrooms.vetDecision.urgen: Any wild mushroom ingestion in small dogs

emergency.ateCookedBones.banner.title: My Dog Ate Cooked Bones: What to Do Now
emergency.ateCookedBones.banner.subtitle: Cooked bones splinter into sharp fragments that can puncture the intestinal wall or cause life-threatening obstruction. This is a mechanical emergency, not a poisoning. Call your vet immediately.
🚨 Vet within 1 hour — hollow bones splinter
emergency.ateCookedBones.steps[0].title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting
emergency.ateCookedBones.steps[0].conten: ⚠️ This is critical: vomiting can cause sharp bone fragments to lodge in the esophagus or puncture tissue on the way back up.
emergency.ateCookedBones.steps[1].title: Offer Soft Food to Cushion Fragments
emergency.ateCookedBones.steps[1].conten: Feed bread, cooked rice, or canned pumpkin to help cushion small bone fragments and reduce injury risk. This does NOT replace veterinary evaluation.
emergency.ateCookedBones.steps[2].title: Call Your Vet for X-Ray Assessment
emergency.ateCookedBones.steps[2].conten: Your vet will X-ray to locate bone fragments, assess obstruction risk, and determine if endoscopic or surgical removal is needed.
emergency.ateCookedBones.steps[3].title: Monitor Stool for 3 Days
emergency.ateCookedBones.steps[3].conten: Watch for: bone fragments in stool (normal passage), black/tarry stool (GI bleeding), inability to defecate (obstruction), or blood. Report any abnormalities to your vet immediately.
emergency.ateCookedBones.science.content: Cooking denatures collagen in bones, making them brittle and prone to splintering. Raw bones contain flexible collagen and are less likely to fragment. When cooked bones splinter, sharp fragments (osteoids) can penetrate the GI wall, causing peritonitis — a life-threatening infection. The most common sites of perforation are the esophagus (if swallowed improperly), stomach, and ileocecal junction (where the small intestine narrows). Poultry bones are especially dangerous because they are hollow and shatter into needle-like shards (AAHA, 2023).
emergency.ateCookedBones.toxicityData.mi: N/A (mechanical hazard — any size fragment can cause damage)
emergency.ateCookedBones.toxicityData.ld: Not applicable — physical trauma, not chemical toxicity
emergency.ateCookedBones.toxicityData.ex: A single chicken bone can shatter into dozens of needle-like splinters that act like tiny knives in the GI tract.
emergency.ateCookedBones.timeline[0].des: Critical window: vet can induce vomiting (if advised) or perform endoscopy. Do NOT induce without professional guidance.
emergency.ateCookedBones.timeline[1].des: Fragments may cause esophageal or stomach perforation. Symptoms: drooling, reluctance to eat, pawing at mouth, vomiting.
emergency.ateCookedBones.timeline[2].des: Intestinal obstruction or perforation symptoms appear: vomiting, no bowel movement, abdominal pain, black tarry stool.
emergency.ateCookedBones.timeline[3].des: If bones passed without complications, no further action needed. If surgery was performed, recovery period.
emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs[0].questio: Why are cooked bones dangerous for dogs?
emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs[0].answer: Cooked bones become brittle and splinter into sharp fragments. These shards can: (1) puncture the esophagus, stomach, or intestinal wall, (2) cause life-threatening peritonitis, (3) create intestinal obstruction, or (4) become lodged in the jaw or throat. Raw bones are safer because they are more flexible, but cooked bones are NEVER safe.
emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs[1].questio: What are the symptoms if my dog ate cooked bones?
emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms of bone-related injury include: vomiting (possibly bloody), diarrhea (may contain blood or look black/tarry), abdominal pain (hunched posture, reluctance to move), difficulty defecating, excessive drooling, pawing at mouth, and lethargy. Symptoms may appear within hours or be delayed 1-3 days if a slow obstruction develops.
emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs[2].questio: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate cooked bones?
emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs[2].answer: Do NOT induce vomiting if your dog ate cooked bones. Regurgitating sharp bone fragments can cause additional damage to the esophagus or become lodged in the throat. Contact your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 for immediate guidance.
emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs[3].questio: What is the treatment for bone ingestion in dogs?
emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs[3].answer: Treatment depends on severity: (1) If bone is lodged in throat/mouth — manual removal under sedation. (2) If bone is in stomach — endoscopic retrieval. (3) If obstruction or perforation — emergency surgery. (4) If small, softened pieces — monitoring with bread/bulk diet to cushion passage. X-rays or ultrasound determine the approach.

emergency.ateCookedBones.vetDecision.urg: Excessive drooling or pawing at mouth

emergency.atePlastic.banner.severityLabe: MONITOR — Obstruction Risk Depends on Size
emergency.atePlastic.banner.title: My Dog Ate Plastic: What to Do Now
emergency.atePlastic.banner.subtitle: Plastic is non-toxic but can cause dangerous intestinal blockage. Risk depends on the size and shape of the object. Call your vet if the piece is larger than 2cm.
emergency.atePlastic.decisionGuide.safe: Plastic piece smaller than 2cm (e.g., corner of wrapper). Monitor stool for 48 hours.
emergency.atePlastic.decisionGuide.call: Plastic piece 2-3cm OR your dog shows ANY vomiting/lethargy. X-ray may be needed.
emergency.atePlastic.decisionGuide.emerg: Plastic larger than 3cm, OR persistent vomiting, OR no bowel movement in 48 hours. Surgery likely needed.
emergency.atePlastic.steps[0].title: Assess the Ingested Object
emergency.atePlastic.steps[0].content: If possible, find the remaining pieces and measure them. Was it a wrapper, toy piece, or bag? Size and shape determine risk.
emergency.atePlastic.steps[1].title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting If Large or Sharp
emergency.atePlastic.steps[1].content: ⚠️ Large objects can lodge in the esophagus; sharp edges can cause damage during regurgitation. Only induce if instructed by a vet for small, smooth items within 30 minutes of ingestion.
emergency.atePlastic.steps[2].title: Feed a Bulk Meal
emergency.atePlastic.steps[2].content: Offer bread, canned pumpkin, or cooked rice to help wrap the plastic and encourage safe passage. This is NOT a substitute for veterinary care if the object is large.
emergency.atePlastic.steps[3].title: Monitor Closely for 48 Hours
emergency.atePlastic.steps[3].content: Check: Is your dog eating? Vomiting? Defecating? Locate the plastic in stool if possible. Absence of bowel movement for 24+ hours with vomiting = emergency.
emergency.atePlastic.science.content: Plastic is chemically inert and non-toxic to dogs — the danger is purely mechanical. The canine GI tract narrows at two critical points: the pylorus (stomach exit, ~1-2cm diameter in small dogs) and the ileocecal junction (small-to-large intestine transition). Objects wider than these passages become lodged, causing a complete or partial obstruction. Complete obstructions cause fluid accumulation, electrolyte imbalances, and intestinal necrosis within 48-72 hours. Surgical intervention is required for objects that do not pass within 24-48 hours or cause persistent vomiting (Merck Veterinary Manual, 2023).
emergency.atePlastic.toxicityData.exampl: A 2cm plastic toy ball will not pass through a medium-sized dog's pylorus. Objects >2cm require vet assessment.
emergency.atePlastic.timeline[0].descrip: Assess the object. If small (<2cm), monitor. If large or sharp, call vet immediately.
emergency.atePlastic.timeline[1].descrip: Small pieces may pass through stomach. Watch for vomiting, lethargy, or abdominal pain.
emergency.atePlastic.timeline[2].descrip: Critical monitoring window. If no bowel movement AND vomiting = possible obstruction. Seek emergency care.
emergency.atePlastic.timeline[3].descrip: If still no bowel movement, X-ray needed to locate blockage. Surgery may be required if object is lodged.
emergency.atePlastic.faqs[0].question: Is plastic dangerous for dogs?
emergency.atePlastic.faqs[0].answer: Plastic is non-toxic but can cause life-threatening intestinal obstruction. The danger depends on the size and shape of the plastic object relative to your dog. Items larger than 2cm wide are unlikely to pass through the pylorus (stomach exit) or ileocecal junction. Sharp plastic edges can also cause GI perforation.
emergency.atePlastic.faqs[1].question: Symptoms of plastic blockage in dogs?
emergency.atePlastic.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 2-48 hours: repeated vomiting (especially after eating), loss of appetite, lethargy, abdominal pain, absence of bowel movements, and dehydration. A complete obstruction causes persistent vomiting, dehydration, and shock within 24-72 hours. This is a surgical emergency.
emergency.atePlastic.faqs[2].question: How long does it take for plastic to pass through a dog?
emergency.atePlastic.faqs[2].answer: Small plastic pieces (under 2cm) typically pass through the GI tract within 24-48 hours and appear in stool. Larger items may take 3-5 days or become lodged. If plastic has not passed within 48 hours, or if vomiting occurs, veterinary intervention is required.
emergency.atePlastic.faqs[3].question: When should I call the vet if my dog ate plastic?
emergency.atePlastic.faqs[3].answer: Call your vet immediately if: (1) the plastic object is larger than 2cm in any dimension, (2) your dog vomits more than once, (3) no bowel movement occurs within 48 hours, (4) your dog shows abdominal pain or lethargy, or (5) the plastic piece is sharp/rigid. Do NOT wait for symptoms if the object is large.
emergency.atePlastic.vetDecision.emergen: Persistent vomiting with no bowel movement
emergency.atePlastic.vetDecision.urgent[: Object 2-3cm and not seen in stool after 24h

emergency.ateMedication.banner.severityL: TOXIC — Human Medication Can Be Fatal to Dogs
emergency.ateMedication.banner.title: My Dog Ate Human Medication: What to Do Now
emergency.ateMedication.banner.subtitle: Human medications are a leading cause of pet poisoning. Even one pill of ibuprofen or acetaminophen can kill a dog. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 IMMEDIATELY.
emergency.ateMedication.riskAssessment.r: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — GI ulcers, kidney failure
emergency.ateMedication.steps[0].title: Gather All Medication Information
emergency.ateMedication.steps[0].content: Bring the pill bottle: drug name, strength (mg), number of pills missing. Calculate total mg consumed: strength × pills. This is critical for toxicity assessment.
emergency.ateMedication.steps[1].title: Call Poison Control IMMEDIATELY
emergency.ateMedication.steps[1].content: ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Do NOT wait for symptoms — some medications cause delayed toxicity.
emergency.ateMedication.steps[2].title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Professional Guidance
emergency.ateMedication.steps[2].content: Some medications are rapidly absorbed; others can cause seizures if vomited. Only induce if ASPCA or your vet instructs you to.
emergency.ateMedication.steps[3].title: Go to Emergency Vet for Decontamination
emergency.ateMedication.steps[3].content: Your vet will induce vomiting (if early), administer activated charcoal, and begin IV fluids. Blood work will monitor liver/kidney function for 24-72 hours.
emergency.ateMedication.science.content: Dogs metabolize many drugs differently than humans. NSAIDs (ibuprofen) inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes, reducing protective prostaglandins in the GI tract and kidneys, leading to ulceration and renal failure. Acetaminophen depletes glutathione in canine hepatocytes and converts hemoglobin to methemoglobin, impairing oxygen transport. Dogs are particularly sensitive to many ADHD medications (amphetamines) due to their effect on catecholamine release. Even "harmless" supplements like vitamin D can cause fatal hypercalcemia when ingested in large amounts (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateMedication.toxicityData.min: Drug-dependent: Ibuprofen 50mg/kg, Acetaminophen 75mg/kg, single pill of some ADHD meds
emergency.ateMedication.toxicityData.exa: A single 200mg ibuprofen tablet can cause kidney failure in a 4kg dog. Five tablets (1000mg) = 250mg/kg = potentially fatal dose.
emergency.ateMedication.timeline[0].desc: Best window for induced vomiting. Call poison control before inducing.
emergency.ateMedication.timeline[1].desc: Drug absorption phase. Symptoms begin for fast-acting drugs (ibuprofen): vomiting, abdominal pain.
emergency.ateMedication.timeline[2].desc: GI ulceration phase (NSAIDs). Symptoms: bloody vomiting, black tarry stool, kidney stress begins.
emergency.ateMedication.timeline[3].desc: Organ damage phase: liver failure (acetaminophen), kidney failure (NSAIDs), seizures (antidepressants). Hospitalization required.
emergency.ateMedication.faqs[0].question: Which human medications are most toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateMedication.faqs[0].answer: The most dangerous human medications for dogs include: (1) NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) — GI ulcers and kidney failure at 50mg/kg. (2) Acetaminophen (Tylenol) — liver damage and methemoglobinemia at 75mg/kg. (3) Antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs) — serotonin syndrome. (4) ADHD medications (amphetamines) — severe stimulation. (5) Benzodiazepines — paradoxical agitation. (6) Vitamin D supplements — fatal hypercalcemia.
emergency.ateMedication.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms of ibuprofen poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateMedication.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 1-4 hours: vomiting (possibly with blood), loss of appetite, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. At toxic doses (50mg/kg+): kidney failure (increased thirst/urination, then decreased urine), GI ulceration, liver damage, and seizures. Megaesophagus (enlarged esophagus) can occur with chronic exposure. Treatment includes activated charcoal, gastroprotectants, IV fluids, and blood monitoring.
emergency.ateMedication.faqs[2].question: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate medication?
emergency.ateMedication.faqs[2].answer: Inducing vomiting may be recommended if ingestion occurred within 30 minutes and your dog is alert. However, do NOT induce vomiting for: caustic substances, if your dog is already symptomatic (seizures, ataxia), or if the medication is rapidly absorbed. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 with the drug name, strength, and estimated number of pills consumed.
emergency.ateMedication.faqs[3].question: How is medication toxicity treated in dogs?
emergency.ateMedication.faqs[3].answer: Treatment depends on the drug: (1) Induced vomiting + activated charcoal (if early), (2) IV fluids for elimination, (3) Gastroprotectants (omeprazole, sucralfate) for NSAIDs, (4) N-acetylcysteine for acetaminophen, (5) Cyproheptadine for serotonin syndrome, (6) Lipid emulsion therapy for fat-soluble drugs. Hospitalization for 24-72 hours is typical for significant ingestions.

emergency.ateRodenticide.steps[0].title: Step 1: This Is a Dire Emergency
emergency.ateRodenticide.steps[0].conten: Do NOT wait for symptoms. Anticoagulant rodenticides have a 2-5 day delay before bleeding begins. By the time symptoms appear, the damage is done. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 NOW.
emergency.ateRodenticide.steps[1].title: Step 2: Bring the Product Package
emergency.ateRodenticide.steps[1].conten: Take the bait package or a photo to the vet. The active ingredient determines treatment: anticoagulants need Vitamin K1; bromethalin needs brain swelling management; cholecalciferol needs calcium-lowering therapy.
emergency.ateRodenticide.steps[2].title: Step 3: Go to Emergency Vet for Decontamination
emergency.ateRodenticide.steps[2].conten: Your vet will induce vomiting (if within 1-2 hours), administer activated charcoal, and start specific antidotes. For anticoagulants: Vitamin K1 for 4-6 weeks with blood clotting tests.
emergency.ateRodenticide.steps[3].title: Step 4: Hospitalization May Be Required
emergency.ateRodenticide.steps[3].conten: Bromethalin poisoning requires 24-72 hour monitoring with mannitol for brain swelling. Anticoagulant cases need plasma transfusions if bleeding is active. Early treatment dramatically improves survival.
emergency.ateRodenticide.science.content: Anticoagulant rodenticides inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR), preventing recycling of vitamin K. This depletes active clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X), causing spontaneous hemorrhage. Second-generation anticoagulants (brodifacoum, bromadiolone) are 100x more potent than warfarin and persist in the liver for weeks. Bromethalin uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in brain cells, causing cerebral edema and increased intracranial pressure. Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) causes hypercalcemia, leading to metastatic calcification of kidneys, heart, and blood vessels (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs[0].questio: Is rat poison deadly to dogs?
emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs[0].answer: Yes, rat poison (rodenticide) is one of the most deadly toxins for dogs. There are two main types: (1) Anticoagulant rodenticides (warfarin, bromadiolone, brodifacoum) — prevent blood clotting, causing fatal internal bleeding. Single-dose types require one feeding; multiple-dose types are cumulative. (2) Neurotoxic rodenticides (bromethalin, strychnine, cholecalciferol) — cause brain swelling, seizures, or hypercalcium within hours. Without treatment, mortality rates are 50-90%.
emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs[1].questio: What are the symptoms of rat poison in dogs?
emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs[1].answer: Anticoagulant symptoms appear 2-5 days after ingestion: weakness, pale gums, coughing blood, bloody vomit/diarrhea, nosebleeds, and collapse. Neurotoxic (bromethalin) symptoms appear within 2-24 hours: severe muscle tremors, seizures, ataxia, and paralysis. Cholecalciferol causes kidney failure with increased thirst/urination within 12-36 hours.
emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs[2].questio: Can my dog survive rat poison?
emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs[2].answer: Yes, with immediate treatment. Anticoagulant poisoning is treatable with Vitamin K1 for 4-6 weeks; survival rate is 80-90% if treated before symptoms appear. Bromethalin has no antidote — treatment is supportive care (activated charcoal, mannitol for brain swelling) with 50-70% survival if treated early. Strychnine and cholecalciferol also require immediate veterinary intervention.
emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs[3].questio: What should I do if my dog ate rat poison?
emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs[3].answer: Treat this as a dire emergency: (1) Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately. (2) Go to the nearest emergency vet NOW — do not wait for symptoms. (3) Bring the product label to identify the active ingredient. (4) Induced vomiting within 1-2 hours may help prevent absorption. (5) Even if your dog seems fine, delayed symptoms are common and early treatment is life-saving.

emergency.ateTobacco.science.content: Nicotine is an alkaloid that binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) in the autonomic ganglia, neuromuscular junctions, and CNS. At low doses, it stimulates receptors causing tachycardia, hypertension, and CNS excitation. At high doses, it causes receptor depolarization blockade, leading to bradycardia, respiratory paralysis, and coma. The biphasic effect (stimulation then depression) is pathognomonic. Dogs metabolize nicotine primarily via hepatic N-oxidation, with a half-life of approximately 1.5 hours. E-liquid poses extreme danger because 1mL can contain 3-24mg of nicotine absorbed rapidly through oral mucosa (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateTobacco.faqs[0].question: How much nicotine is toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateTobacco.faqs[0].answer: The toxic dose of nicotine in dogs is 20-100mg/kg. For a 20kg dog, this equals 400-2000mg of nicotine. Sources: 1 cigarette = 10-15mg nicotine, 1 cigarette butt = 5-7mg, nicotine patch = 8-21mg, nicotine gum = 2-4mg, e-liquid = 3-24mg/mL (highly concentrated). Even ONE cigarette can cause symptoms in a small dog.
emergency.ateTobacco.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms of nicotine poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateTobacco.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 15-60 minutes: hypersalivation, vomiting, tachycardia (rapid heart rate), muscle tremors, agitation, and hypertension. As toxicity progresses: bradycardia (slow heart rate), weakness, collapse, respiratory paralysis, and seizures. The biphasic effect — first excitation then depression — is characteristic of nicotine poisoning.
emergency.ateTobacco.faqs[2].question: Is vape liquid dangerous for dogs?
emergency.ateTobacco.faqs[2].answer: Yes, e-liquid (vape juice) is EXTREMELY dangerous due to high nicotine concentration. A single 10mL bottle can contain 30-240mg of nicotine — enough to kill multiple small dogs. The sweet flavorings also attract dogs. Ingestion of even small amounts requires emergency veterinary treatment.
emergency.ateTobacco.faqs[3].question: What should I do if my dog ate tobacco?
emergency.ateTobacco.faqs[3].answer: Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately. Calculate total nicotine consumed: mg per item × number of items. Go to emergency vet if your dog ingested: (1) more than 1 cigarette, (2) any e-liquid, (3) a nicotine patch, or (4) any amount if your dog shows symptoms. Do NOT induce vomiting if seizures or tremors are present.

emergency.ateMarijuana.banner.subtitle: Dogs are more sensitive to THC than humans. Edibles (gummies, brownies) are especially dangerous due to high concentration. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435.
emergency.ateMarijuana.honestySection.ti: 📋 Important: Be Honest With Your Vet
emergency.ateMarijuana.honestySection.co: Veterinarians are required to treat, not report, pet poisonings. Accurate information about marijuana ingestion ensures your dog receives proper care without unnecessary testing. Your honesty is protected and helps save your dog's life.
emergency.ateMarijuana.riskAssessment.ro: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — high THC + chocolate
📞 May also contain xylitol — call vet
emergency.ateMarijuana.steps[0].title: Step 1: Remove All Remaining Product
emergency.ateMarijuana.steps[0].content: Check for packaging — note THC content in mg per piece and total pieces eaten. This determines toxicity risk.
emergency.ateMarijuana.steps[1].title: Step 2: Check for Xylitol (CBD Products)
emergency.ateMarijuana.steps[1].content: ⚠️ Some CBD oils contain xylitol, which is extremely toxic to dogs. Check the ingredient list immediately.
emergency.ateMarijuana.steps[2].title: Step 3: Call Poison Control or Vet
emergency.ateMarijuana.steps[2].content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Be honest — they will provide guidance without judgment.
emergency.ateMarijuana.steps[3].title: Step 4: Monitor Symptoms
emergency.ateMarijuana.steps[3].content: Watch for: stumbling, dilated pupils, urinary incontinence, drooling, slow heart rate, hypothermia. Severe cases: seizures or coma. Symptoms can last 12-72 hours.
emergency.ateMarijuana.science.content: Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) binds to CB1 cannabinoid receptors in the canine central nervous system. Dogs have a higher density of CB1 receptors in the cerebellum (responsible for coordination) and brainstem than humans, explaining their heightened sensitivity. THC is lipophilic and undergoes enterohepatic recirculation, prolonging effects. Edibles are dangerous because the GI tract absorbs THC rapidly, and the liver converts 11-hydroxy-THC, which is 5x more psychoactive. Most cases are supportive — there is no specific antidote, but IV lipid emulsion therapy can accelerate THC clearance (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs[0].question: Is marijuana toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs[0].answer: Yes, THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) is toxic to dogs. Dogs have more cannabinoid receptors (CB1) in the brain than humans, making them significantly more sensitive. Edibles (gummies, brownies, cookies) are especially dangerous due to high THC concentration — one gummy can contain 10-100mg THC, which is toxic to most dogs.
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms of marijuana poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 30-90 minutes: dazed appearance, stumbling/ataxia, urinary incontinence (dripping urine), drooling, dilated pupils, vomiting, tremors, bradycardia (slow heart rate), hypothermia, and in severe cases: seizures or coma. Be honest with your vet — marijuana toxicosis is rarely fatal, and honesty ensures proper treatment.
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs[2].question: Are marijuana edibles more dangerous than dried cannabis?
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs[2].answer: Yes, edibles are significantly more dangerous: (1) High THC concentration (10-100mg per piece), (2) Often contain chocolate (double toxicity), (3) Faster absorption from GI tract, (4) Dogs eat multiple pieces quickly. Edibles account for the majority of severe cannabis toxicosis cases in dogs.
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs[3].question: Can a dog die from eating marijuana?
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs[3].answer: Fatalities from marijuana alone are rare in dogs — the LD50 is very high (over 3g/kg of THC). However, edibles pose additional risks: chocolate toxicity, xylitol in some CBD products, and overdose from multiple ingestion. Death is more likely from complications (aspiration pneumonia, hypothermia) or combined toxins. Always seek veterinary care.
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs[4].question: Should I tell my vet my dog ate marijuana?
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs[4].answer: Yes, always be honest. Veterinarians are required to treat, not report, pet poisonings. Knowing your dog ate marijuana ensures they provide appropriate care: inducing vomiting (if early), activated charcoal, IV fluids, thermoregulation, and monitoring heart rate. Without this information, your dog may undergo unnecessary tests or receive inappropriate treatment.

emergency.ateXylitolGum.banner.title: My Dog Ate Xylitol Gum: What to Do Now
emergency.ateXylitolGum.banner.subtitle: Xylitol triggers a massive insulin release causing life-threatening hypoglycemia and liver failure. One piece of gum can kill a small dog. Go to emergency vet NOW.
emergency.ateXylitolGum.riskAssessment.r: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — liver failure too
emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps[0].title: Step 1: Calculate Total Xylitol Consumed
emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps[0].content: Find the packaging. Xylitol content is listed in grams per piece. Calculate: grams per piece × pieces eaten. This determines whether hypoglycemia risk (0.1g/kg) or liver failure risk (0.5g/kg) threshold is crossed.
emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps[1].title: Step 2: Call Poison Control and Go to Emergency Vet
emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps[1].content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Do NOT wait for symptoms — hypoglycemia can cause death within hours. Xylitol is absorbed rapidly.
emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps[2].title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Vet Approval
emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps[2].content: ⚠️ If instructed to induce at home, use hydrogen peroxide (1 tsp per 5lbs). But go to vet ASAP — xylitol may need IV dextrose to prevent hypoglycemia.
emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps[3].title: Step 4: Prepare for Hospitalization
emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps[3].content: Your vet will: induce vomiting (if early), give activated charcoal, start IV dextrose, and monitor blood glucose for 24 hours. Liver enzymes will be checked for 72 hours. Early treatment has 80%+ survival.
emergency.ateXylitolGum.science.content: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol (polyol) that triggers a rapid, exaggerated insulin release from canine beta cells — up to 6-7x the amount released by glucose. This is because dogs metabolize xylitol via the same pathway as glucose but with different kinetics. The resulting hypoglycemia (blood glucose <60mg/dL) causes neurological dysfunction, seizures, and death. At higher doses (>0.5g/kg), xylitol causes acute hepatic necrosis through ATP depletion and oxidative stress. The mechanism is dose-dependent and unique to dogs — cats appear to be less susceptible (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs[0].question: How much xylitol is toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs[0].answer: Xylitol is toxic to dogs at doses as low as 0.1g/kg for hypoglycemia and 0.5g/kg for liver failure. A single piece of sugar-free gum can contain 0.3-1.0g of xylitol — meaning ONE piece can cause severe hypoglycemia in a small-to-medium dog. Emergency treatment is needed even for tiny amounts.
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms of xylitol poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 10-60 minutes (sometimes delayed 12 hours): vomiting, lethargy, weakness, collapse, tremors, seizures, and coma — these result from hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). Liver failure symptoms (jaundice, coagulopathy) may be delayed 12-72 hours. Even small amounts cause dangerously low blood sugar.
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs[2].question: Why is xylitol toxic to dogs but not humans?
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs[2].answer: In dogs, xylitol is rapidly absorbed and triggers a massive insulin release from the pancreas — 6-7x more than glucose would. This causes profound hypoglycemia. Humans do not have this insulin response. Additionally, xylitol causes dose-dependent hepatocellular necrosis in dogs through mechanisms not seen in humans.
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs[3].question: What products contain xylitol?
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs[3].answer: Xylitol is found in: sugar-free gum, mints, peanut butter (some brands), toothpaste, mouthwash, nasal sprays, chewable vitamins, baked goods, ice cream, and "birch sugar" sold as a sweetener. Some brands: Trident, Orbit, Ice Breakers, Eclipse. Always check ingredient lists before giving human food to dogs.
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs[4].question: Can a dog survive xylitol poisoning?
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs[4].answer: Yes, with immediate treatment. If caught within 30 minutes, induced vomiting prevents absorption. If hypoglycemia has begun, IV dextrose corrects blood sugar. Even with liver damage, aggressive hospital care (IV fluids, liver protectants, plasma transfusions) has 70-80% survival if treatment begins within 8 hours. Delayed treatment has worse prognosis.

emergency.ateChocolate.banner.subtitle: Chocolate contains theobromine, which dogs cannot metabolize effectively. Immediate action is critical — call your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 right away.
emergency.ateChocolate.steps[0].title: Call for Help Immediately
emergency.ateChocolate.steps[0].content: Contact ASPCA Animal Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 or your nearest emergency vet. Time is critical — do not wait for symptoms to appear.
emergency.ateChocolate.steps[1].title: Gather Information
emergency.ateChocolate.steps[1].content: Note the type of chocolate (milk, dark, baking), estimated amount consumed, and your dog's weight. This helps the vet assess toxicity risk.
emergency.ateChocolate.steps[2].title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Vet Approval
emergency.ateChocolate.steps[2].content: Inducing vomiting can cause aspiration pneumonia or worsen the situation. Only do so if explicitly instructed by a veterinarian.
emergency.ateChocolate.steps[3].title: Monitor Symptoms Closely
emergency.ateChocolate.steps[3].content: Watch for vomiting, diarrhea, restlessness, increased thirst, rapid breathing, and seizures. Symptoms may appear within 2-4 hours.
emergency.ateChocolate.science.content: Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, both methylxanthines that dogs metabolize much more slowly than humans. While humans eliminate theobromine in 2-3 hours, dogs take 17.5 hours or more. This allows toxic levels to build up in their system. Theobromine affects the central nervous system, cardiovascular system, and smooth muscles. At high doses, it causes seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, and potentially death (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateChocolate.faqs[0].question: How much chocolate is toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateChocolate.faqs[0].answer: Toxicity depends on the type of chocolate and your dog's weight. Milk chocolate becomes toxic at approximately 0.5 oz per pound of body weight. Dark chocolate is 2-3x more toxic. Baking chocolate is the most dangerous — as little as 0.1 oz per pound can be lethal. Use our toxicity calculator to assess your dog's specific risk.
emergency.ateChocolate.faqs[1].question: How long after eating chocolate will a dog show symptoms?
emergency.ateChocolate.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms typically appear within 2-4 hours but can be delayed up to 12 hours. Early signs include vomiting, diarrhea, and restlessness. Severe symptoms (seizures, irregular heartbeat) may appear 6-12 hours after ingestion. Theobromine is absorbed slowly, so symptoms can worsen over time.
emergency.ateChocolate.faqs[2].question: Can a dog die from eating chocolate?
emergency.ateChocolate.faqs[2].answer: Yes, chocolate can be fatal to dogs. The lethal dose of theobromine is approximately 100-500 mg per kg of body weight. For a 20kg (44lb) dog, this equals roughly 200g of milk chocolate or 100g of dark chocolate. Immediate veterinary treatment significantly improves survival rates.

emergency.ateGrapes.banner.subtitle: Grapes and raisins can cause acute kidney failure in dogs. Even small amounts are dangerous — call your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately.
emergency.ateGrapes.steps[0].title: Call Your Vet Immediately
emergency.ateGrapes.steps[0].content: Contact your veterinarian or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 right away. Do not wait for symptoms to appear.
emergency.ateGrapes.steps[1].title: Note the Amount
emergency.ateGrapes.steps[1].content: Record how many grapes or raisins your dog ate and their weight. This helps determine toxicity risk.
emergency.ateGrapes.steps[2].title: Vet May Induce Vomiting
emergency.ateGrapes.steps[2].content: If ingestion was recent (within 2 hours), your vet may induce vomiting or administer activated charcoal to prevent absorption.
emergency.ateGrapes.steps[3].title: Monitor for 72 Hours
emergency.ateGrapes.steps[3].content: Kidney damage may not show symptoms immediately. Watch for vomiting, lethargy, decreased urination, and loss of appetite.
emergency.ateGrapes.science.content: The exact toxic compound in grapes and raisins remains unidentified, but tartaric acid is the leading suspect. This compound causes acute tubular necrosis in the kidneys, leading to rapid kidney failure. The toxic dose is unpredictable — some dogs develop kidney failure from just a few grapes, while others tolerate more. This variability makes any ingestion a medical emergency (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateGrapes.faqs[0].question: How many grapes are toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateGrapes.faqs[0].answer: The toxic dose is not established, but as few as 1-2 grapes can cause kidney failure in some dogs. Raisins are more concentrated and thus more dangerous. There is no known safe amount — any ingestion should be treated as an emergency.
emergency.ateGrapes.faqs[1].question: How long after eating grapes do symptoms appear?
emergency.ateGrapes.faqs[1].answer: Vomiting and diarrhea typically begin within 6-12 hours. Signs of kidney failure (decreased urination, lethargy, loss of appetite) may not appear until 24-72 hours after ingestion. Early veterinary intervention is critical.
emergency.ateGrapes.faqs[2].question: Why are grapes toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateGrapes.faqs[2].answer: The exact toxic mechanism is still unknown. Tartaric acid is the suspected toxin, with varying concentrations between grape varieties. This unpredictability makes any grape ingestion potentially dangerous.

emergency.ateXylitol.steps[0].content: Xylitol acts fast. Contact your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately — do not wait for symptoms.

emergency.ateXylitol.steps[2].content: Your vet will likely induce vomiting (if within 1 hour), start IV dextrose, and monitor liver enzymes for 72 hours.
emergency.ateXylitol.steps[3].title: Do NOT Wait for Symptoms
emergency.ateXylitol.steps[3].content: By the time symptoms appear (vomiting, lethargy, seizures), treatment may be less effective. Early intervention saves lives.
emergency.ateXylitol.science.content: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that triggers a rapid, massive insulin release from the dog's pancreas. This causes blood sugar to plummet within 10-30 minutes. At higher doses, xylitol causes acute liver failure through mechanisms that are not fully understood. Unlike humans, dogs absorb xylitol rapidly and their bodies mistake it for real sugar, triggering this dangerous insulin response (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateXylitol.faqs[0].question: How much xylitol is toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateXylitol.faqs[0].answer: As little as 0.1g of xylitol per kg of body weight can cause hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). Doses above 0.5g/kg can cause acute liver failure. A single piece of sugar-free gum can contain 0.3-1g of xylitol — potentially lethal for a small dog.
emergency.ateXylitol.faqs[1].question: How fast does xylitol affect dogs?
emergency.ateXylitol.faqs[1].answer: Hypoglycemia can develop within 10-30 minutes of ingestion. Liver damage may take 8-12 hours to manifest. Rapid treatment is essential — do not wait for symptoms.
emergency.ateXylitol.faqs[2].question: Where is xylitol found?
emergency.ateXylitol.faqs[2].answer: Xylitol is found in sugar-free gum, candy, baked goods, peanut butter, toothpaste, mouthwash, and some medications. Always check labels — it may be listed as 'birch sugar' or 'xylitol'.

emergency.ateOnion.steps[0].title: Call Your Vet
emergency.ateOnion.steps[0].content: Contact your veterinarian or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435. Note the amount and type of onion consumed.
emergency.ateOnion.steps[1].title: Vet May Induce Vomiting
emergency.ateOnion.steps[1].content: If ingestion was recent (within 2 hours), your vet may induce vomiting to prevent further absorption of thiosulfate compounds.
emergency.ateOnion.steps[2].title: Monitor for Anemia Symptoms
emergency.ateOnion.steps[2].content: Watch for weakness, pale gums, rapid breathing, and reddish-brown urine over the next 1-3 days.
emergency.ateOnion.steps[3].title: Blood Work May Be Needed
emergency.ateOnion.steps[3].content: Your vet may recommend a CBC blood test to check for Heinz body anemia, which confirms onion toxicity.
emergency.ateOnion.science.content: Onions contain thiosulfate compounds (n-propyl disulfide) that dogs cannot metabolize. These compounds cause oxidative damage to red blood cells, forming Heinz bodies — damaged hemoglobin that precipitates inside the cell. The spleen then destroys these damaged cells, leading to hemolytic anemia. This process takes 1-3 days, which is why symptoms are delayed (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateOnion.faqs[0].question: How much onion is toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateOnion.faqs[0].answer: Onion toxicity occurs at approximately 0.5% of the dog's body weight. For a 20kg (44lb) dog, this equals about 100g (3.5oz) of onion. All forms are toxic: raw, cooked, powdered, and dehydrated. Onion powder is especially concentrated and dangerous.
emergency.ateOnion.faqs[1].question: How long after eating onion do symptoms appear?
emergency.ateOnion.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms typically develop 1-3 days after ingestion as red blood cells are progressively destroyed. Early signs include weakness, pale gums, and reddish urine. Severe cases can lead to collapse and require blood transfusion.
emergency.ateOnion.faqs[2].question: Are all onion types toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateOnion.faqs[2].answer: Yes — all Allium species are toxic: onions, garlic, leeks, chives, and shallots. Garlic is less toxic per gram but still dangerous in quantity. Cooking does not reduce toxicity. Onion powder is the most concentrated form.

emergency.ateSock.banner.subtitle: Socks can cause life-threatening intestinal blockages in dogs. Do not wait — call your vet immediately for assessment and possible intervention.
emergency.ateSock.steps[0].title: Call Your Vet Immediately
emergency.ateSock.steps[0].content: Contact your veterinarian right away. Note when the sock was eaten and your dog's size — this determines urgency.
emergency.ateSock.steps[1].title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting
emergency.ateSock.steps[1].content: Unlike toxins, foreign objects can cause more damage coming back up. Only induce vomiting if your vet explicitly instructs you to.
emergency.ateSock.steps[2].title: Vet May Retrieve Endoscopically
emergency.ateSock.steps[2].content: If the sock is still in the stomach (within 12-24 hours), your vet may remove it via endoscopy — a non-surgical procedure using a camera and grabber.
emergency.ateSock.steps[3].title: Monitor for Blockage Signs
emergency.ateSock.steps[3].content: Watch for vomiting after eating, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, lethargy, and inability to defecate. These require emergency surgery.
emergency.ateSock.science.content: Fabric foreign bodies are particularly dangerous because they can become lodged at the pyloric sphincter (stomach exit) or in the small intestine. Once stuck, they cause a complete blockage — nothing can pass, and the intestinal wall may become necrotic (die) from pressure. This leads to perforation, peritonitis, and death without surgical intervention. Puppies and small dogs are at highest risk due to their narrower intestinal diameter (AVMA, 2023).
emergency.ateSock.faqs[0].question: Will my dog pass a sock naturally?
emergency.ateSock.faqs[0].answer: Small socks may pass through the digestive tract within 24-48 hours, but this is not guaranteed. Larger socks or those that become lodged can cause life-threatening intestinal blockage. Never wait to see if it passes — consult your vet immediately.
emergency.ateSock.faqs[1].question: How long after eating a sock will symptoms appear?
emergency.ateSock.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms of intestinal blockage typically appear within 2-24 hours. Watch for vomiting (especially after eating), loss of appetite, abdominal pain, lethargy, and inability to defecate. These are emergency signs.
emergency.ateSock.faqs[2].question: What is the treatment for sock ingestion?
emergency.ateSock.faqs[2].answer: Treatment depends on location and size. Your vet may induce vomiting (if within 2 hours), perform endoscopy to retrieve the object, or conduct abdominal surgery if the sock has caused a blockage. X-rays and ultrasound help determine the best approach.

emergency.ateAntifreeze.banner.subtitle: Antifreeze (ethylene glycol) causes rapid kidney failure and death. As little as 1 teaspoon can kill — call your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 IMMEDIATELY.
emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps[0].title: EMERGENCY VET NOW
emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps[0].content: Go to the nearest emergency vet immediately. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 en route. Every minute counts.
emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps[1].title: Do NOT Wait for Symptoms
emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps[1].content: By the time symptoms appear, kidney damage may be irreversible. The antidote must be given within 8-12 hours to be effective.
emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps[2].title: Bring the Container
emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps[2].content: Take the antifreeze container to the vet. This confirms the active ingredient (ethylene glycol) and concentration.
emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps[3].title: Treatment Window is Critical
emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps[3].content: Your vet will administer fomepizole (4-MP) or ethanol IV to block metabolism. After 12 hours, treatment is much less effective.
emergency.ateAntifreeze.science.content: Ethylene glycol itself is not toxic — it is the metabolites produced by the liver that cause damage. Alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethylene glycol to glycoaldehyde, then glycolic acid, then oxalic acid. Oxalic acid binds with calcium to form calcium oxalate crystals that destroy kidney tissue. This process causes metabolic acidosis and acute kidney failure within 12-36 hours. The antidote works by blocking alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing toxic metabolite formation (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateAntifreeze.faqs[0].question: How much antifreeze is lethal to dogs?
emergency.ateAntifreeze.faqs[0].answer: As little as 1 teaspoon (5ml) of antifreeze can kill a 10lb (4.5kg) dog. The lethal dose of ethylene glycol is approximately 4.4ml per kg of body weight. This makes antifreeze one of the most dangerous household toxins for pets.
emergency.ateAntifreeze.faqs[1].question: How fast does antifreeze kill dogs?
emergency.ateAntifreeze.faqs[1].answer: Without treatment, antifreeze is fatal within 12-36 hours. The antidote (fomepizole or ethanol) must be administered within 8-12 hours of ingestion to be effective. After kidney failure begins, survival rates drop dramatically.
emergency.ateAntifreeze.faqs[2].question: What are the symptoms of antifreeze poisoning?
emergency.ateAntifreeze.faqs[2].answer: Stage 1 (30 min-12 hrs): drunken behavior, vomiting, seizures. Stage 2 (12-24 hrs): apparent improvement (misleading). Stage 3 (24-72 hrs): kidney failure, severe lethargy, mouth ulcers, coma. Early treatment is critical.

catEmergency.ateChocolate.steps[1].conte: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Cats are more sensitive to theobromine than dogs — small amounts are concerning.
catEmergency.ateChocolate.steps[2].title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Vet Approval
catEmergency.ateChocolate.steps[2].conte: ⚠️ Cats may hide symptoms until severe. Inducing vomiting risks aspiration. Only do so if instructed by a veterinarian.
catEmergency.ateChocolate.steps[3].title: Step 4: Go to Vet for Cardiac Monitoring
catEmergency.ateChocolate.steps[3].conte: Your vet may recommend induced vomiting (if early), activated charcoal, and ECG monitoring to watch for arrhythmias.
catEmergency.ateChocolate.science.conten: Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine — methylxanthines that cats cannot efficiently metabolize. Cytochrome P450 enzymes in feline liver have reduced activity compared to dogs, causing prolonged theobromine half-life. This leads to cumulative effects on the CNS (seizures), cardiovascular system (arrhythmias), and smooth muscles. Cats are also obligate carnivores with less capacity to process plant-derived alkaloids. The combination of smaller body weight, slower metabolism, and greater sensitivity makes chocolate proportionally more dangerous for cats (ASPCA, 2023).
catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs[0].answer: Yes, chocolate is toxic to cats — often more so than to dogs relative to body weight. Cats are more sensitive to theobromine because they metabolize it more slowly. The same toxic principle applies: theobromine and caffeine cause CNS stimulation, cardiac arrhythmias, and potentially seizures.
catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs[1].questi: Why are cats more sensitive than dogs?
catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs[1].answer: Cats have lower activity of cytochrome P450 enzymes responsible for metabolizing theobromine. While dogs take 17+ hours to clear theobromine, cats may take even longer. Additionally, cats typically weigh less (4-6kg average), so the dose-per-kg ratio from the same amount of chocolate is higher.
catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs[2].questi: How much chocolate is toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs[2].answer: Milk chocolate becomes toxic at approximately 0.5 oz per pound of body weight. Dark chocolate and baking chocolate are 2-5x more toxic. For a 5kg (11lb) cat, as little as 20g of milk chocolate (about half a standard bar) can cause symptoms. Baking chocolate is lethal at 5-10g for an average cat.
catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs[3].questi: What should I do if my cat ate chocolate?
catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs[3].answer: Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 or your vet immediately. Cats are more sensitive than dogs — even small amounts are concerning. Bring the chocolate packaging to identify theobromine content. Do NOT wait for symptoms, as cardiac arrhythmias can be sudden and fatal.

catEmergency.ateOnion.steps[0].title: Step 1: Note the Type and Amount
catEmergency.ateOnion.steps[0].content: Was it raw onion, cooked onion, onion powder, or a product containing onion? Powder is most concentrated. Calculate approximate amount.
catEmergency.ateOnion.steps[1].title: Step 2: Call Vet or Poison Control
catEmergency.ateOnion.steps[1].content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Even small amounts can cause delayed anemia — early blood work may be needed.
catEmergency.ateOnion.steps[2].title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Unless Instructed
catEmergency.ateOnion.steps[2].content: ⚠️ Symptoms are delayed 1-5 days. Induction is not effective after absorption. Your vet may induce vomiting if ingestion was very recent.
catEmergency.ateOnion.steps[3].title: Step 4: Schedule Blood Work
catEmergency.ateOnion.steps[3].content: Your vet will check for Heinz bodies and monitor red blood cell count for 3-5 days. Early detection of anemia allows transfusion if needed.
catEmergency.ateOnion.science.content: Onions (Allium cepa) contain N-propyl disulfide and S-methylcysteine sulfoxide. These compounds cause oxidative damage to hemoglobin, forming Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin precipitates). The spleen removes damaged cells, causing hemolytic anemia. Cats are especially vulnerable because feline hemoglobin contains more sulfhydryl groups than other species, making it more susceptible to oxidation. Additionally, cats have lower glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) activity, reducing their ability to protect red blood cells from oxidative injury. Anemia typically peaks 3-5 days post-ingestion (Merck Veterinary Manual, 2023).
catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs[0].question: Are onions toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs[0].answer: Yes, onions are highly toxic to cats — more so than dogs relative to body weight. Onions contain N-propyl disulfide and thiosulfates that cause oxidative damage to red blood cells, leading to Heinz body hemolytic anemia. Cats are uniquely vulnerable because their hemoglobin is more susceptible to oxidation, and they produce methemoglobin more readily.
catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs[1].question: How much onion is toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs[1].answer: Even small amounts are dangerous. Toxic effects can occur at 5g/kg body weight (about 1 tablespoon for a 4kg cat). Regular consumption of smaller amounts (even trace amounts in baby food or broth) can cause cumulative damage. Raw, cooked, powdered, and dehydrated onions are all toxic.
catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs[2].question: What are the symptoms of onion poisoning in cats?
catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs[2].answer: Symptoms appear 1-5 days after ingestion: pale or yellow gums (anemia/jaundice), weakness, rapid breathing, reddish-brown urine (hemoglobinuria), vomiting, and lethargy. Heinz body anemia is confirmed by blood smear showing damaged red blood cells. Severe cases require blood transfusion.
catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs[3].question: Can onion powder hurt cats?
catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs[3].answer: Yes, onion powder is concentrated and especially dangerous. Even small amounts in broth, gravy, baby food, or treats can cause toxicity. Many commercial products contain hidden onion or garlic powder. Always check ingredient labels before sharing human food with cats.

catEmergency.ateGarlic.science.content: Garlic (Allium sativum) contains alliin, which converts to allicin when crushed or chewed. Allicin and its derivatives (allyl propyl disulfide, ajoene) cause oxidative denaturation of hemoglobin in feline erythrocytes. The feline hemoglobin molecule has 8-10 sulfhydryl groups (vs 2-4 in dogs), making it 2-3x more susceptible to oxidative damage. The resulting Heinz bodies are phagocytosed by splenic macrophages, causing extravascular hemolysis. Unlike onions, garlic's thiosulfates are more bioavailable in cats due to differences in hepatic metabolism (Merck Veterinary Manual, 2023).
catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs[0].question: Is garlic toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs[0].answer: Yes, garlic is highly toxic to cats — approximately 5x more potent than onion per gram. Garlic (Allium sativum) contains allicin, alliin, and allyl propyl disulfide, which cause severe oxidative damage to feline red blood cells. Cats are uniquely susceptible due to the structure of their hemoglobin molecule.
catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs[1].question: How much garlic is toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs[1].answer: As little as 5g of garlic per kg of body weight can cause toxicity. For a 4kg cat, this equals just 1 small clove (approximately 5g). Toxic effects can also occur from chronic low-dose exposure — even trace amounts in food or supplements over weeks can accumulate and cause anemia.
catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs[2].question: Is garlic salt/powder dangerous for cats?
catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs[2].answer: Yes, garlic powder and salt are concentrated forms. As little as 1/8 teaspoon of garlic powder can be toxic to a small cat. Dry garlic powder, garlic supplements, garlic-flavored treats, and garlic-infused oils all pose risks. Many human foods contain hidden garlic — always check labels.
catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs[3].question: What are the symptoms of garlic poisoning in cats?
catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs[3].answer: Symptoms develop 1-5 days after ingestion: pale gums (anemia), lethargy, weakness, rapid breathing, elevated heart rate, jaundice (yellow gums/eyes), reddish-brown urine, vomiting, and collapse. Heinz body anemia is confirmed by blood smear. Severe cases require blood transfusions.

catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.steps[0].t: Step 1: Wash Your Cat If Oil Is On Fur/Skin
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.steps[0].c: Use Dawn dish soap (cuts oil) to wash off any topical exposure. Rinse thoroughly. Do NOT use water alone — oil repels water.
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.steps[1].c: Turn off diffusers, remove oil containers, and ventilate the area. Move your cat to fresh air.
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.steps[2].c: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Bring the oil bottle — tell them the botanical name and phenol/terpene content if listed.
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.steps[3].c: ⚠️ Essential oils have high aspiration pneumonia risk. Vomiting can cause oil to enter lungs. Go to vet for safe decontamination.
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.science.co: Cats lack UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A6 and UGT1A9) enzymes required for phase II glucuronidation of terpenes (d-limonene, alpha-terpineol) and phenols (eugenol, thymol). These compounds accumulate in the hepatobiliary system, causing hepatotoxicity and neurotoxicity. Cats also have deficient P-glycoprotein efflux transporters at the blood-brain barrier, increasing CNS exposure. Tea tree oil (Melaleuca alternifolia) monoterpenes cause dose-dependent CNS depression, ataxia, and hypothermia. Even 10mL applied dermally can be fatal in cats (ASPCA, 2023).
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs[0].qu: Why are essential oils toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs[0].an: Cats lack UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) enzymes needed to metabolize certain compounds in essential oils (terpenes, phenols, ketones). This makes them 10x more sensitive than dogs to tea tree oil, citrus oils, eucalyptus, peppermint, and pine oils. Even topical application on skin can cause toxicity if the cat licks it off.
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs[1].qu: Which essential oils are most dangerous for cats?
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs[1].an: Most dangerous: Tea tree (melaleuca), wintergreen, peppermint, pine, eucalyptus, citrus (limonene, linalool), cinnamon, clove, ylang ylang, birch, and thyme. Tea tree oil is most commonly reported — even 10-20mL on skin can be fatal. Diffusers are also dangerous as cats inhale droplets and groom them from fur.
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs[2].qu: What are the symptoms of essential oil poisoning in cats?
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs[2].an: Symptoms depend on oil type and route: (1) Ingestion: drooling, vomiting, tremors, ataxia, weakness, hypothermia. (2) Skin absorption: lethargy, hypersalivation, liver damage. (3) Inhalation: respiratory distress, aspiration pneumonia. Tea tree oil specifically causes severe hypothermia and ataxia within 2-8 hours.
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs[3].qu: Are essential oil diffusers dangerous for cats?
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs[3].an: Yes, diffusers pose three risks: (1) Inhaled droplets settle on fur and are groomed off, causing ingestion. (2) Volatilized oils irritate feline respiratory passages (cats have efficient smell but sensitive airways). (3) Concentrated oil in the diffuser water can be spilled and licked. Use diffusers only in well-ventilated rooms your cat cannot access.
